title: The young entrepreneurs ditching university degrees for Silicon Valley success
detail:
The young entrepreneurs ditching university degrees for Silicon Valley success
Erik Olsson
Mon, September 14, 2026 at 3:00 AM MST 7 min read
ABNB
Trade Airbnb on Coinbase
Trading disclosure
Theo Kitsberg, 22, is the co-founder of AI-powered recruitment firm Prism - Geoff Pugh/The Telegraph

Theo Kitsberg had just finished the second year of his Cambridge philosophy degree when he was offered $500,000 (£370,000) to drop out.

The 20-year-old was presented with the proposal by Tom Blomfield, the multimillionaire founder and former chief executive of online bank Monzo.

"He phoned me up to say: 'Hey, would you guys like to leave university and come to San Francisco?'" Kitsberg, now 22, says.

He and his business partner, Axel La Pira, were interviewed by Blomfield after applying for seed funding from Y Combinator (YC) – a Silicon Valley institution which helped launch household names such as Reddit, Airbnb and Door Dash – for Prism, their AI-powered recruitment firm.

YC runs a three-month programme in San Francisco, where aspiring tech founders are given the mentorship and six-figure investment needed to launch their businesses.

Against a backdrop of near-record youth worklessness, Kitsberg belongs to a growing cohort of young aspiring British entrepreneurs who are upping sticks and hoping to move to the United States, where the opportunities are plentiful and the salaries can be stratospheric.

Some, like Kitsberg, are even leaving behind prestigious degrees or top graduate jobs to do so.

Kitsberg says: "You just fill out a form on their website, which can take around half an hour, and then you get selected for interview – it's literally a 10-minute interview – and that's what they use to decide if you get half a million dollars.

"The process felt surprisingly quick for what felt like a lot of money, and for something that definitely has changed my life."

Kitsberg is now in the process of securing his visa and hopes to relocate to the US - Geoff Pugh/The Telegraph

YC, a venture capital firm, takes a fixed 7pc stake in return for the first $125,000 of the cash injection in a business, with the size of the second stake on the remaining $375,000 dependent on fundraising from other investors.

Kitsberg, who is in the process of securing his visa to relocate to the US, has now raised more than $3m for his business after quitting Cambridge in 2025.

He says it was a straightforward decision to leave the storied institution, despite holding a college scholarship and achieving first class results in his first year.

He had seen others build companies that scaled "very, very quickly", he said, so he was certain that he had made the right choice to drop out.

Kitsberg initially asked Cambridge whether he could take a year out from his degree, but he was told this would not be an option. He would either have to stay or leave.

"By the time they came back with [the ultimatum], I had already committed anyway," he says.

Airbnb's AI cut customer support costs 16%, resolved 45% of tickets without agents, and expanded adjusted EBITDA margins to 35%.

Airbnb outpaced Booking's 8% and Expedia's 14% revenue growth, but both rivals are deploying identical AI tools, threatening Airbnb's lead.

Airbnb (NASDAQ:ABNB) CEO Brian Chesky told CNBC's David Faber at Goldman Sachs' technology conference this week that AI is the best thing to happen to his company. Most executives who make that claim offer vibes, but Chesky backed it up with numbers.

Gorodenkoff / Shutterstock.com

He said Airbnb is shipping 80% more software than a year ago, and that almost half of customer service tickets are now handled by AI. He also argued that the long-run economic value of AI will accrue to the companies applying it, comparing the technology to electricity.

Airbnb's Q2 2026 receipts are strong, though shipping velocity and deflected tickets are input metrics. The real question for you as an investor is whether the AI story shows up where it matters: bookings, take rate, and margin.

Receipts Behind the AI Boast

Chesky's operating claims track what Airbnb reported for the quarter. Revenue rose 16.54% to $3.608 billion, net income climbed 27.1% to $816 million, and free cash flow jumped 31.62%.

The AI-specific evidence is clearer than most companies produce. Airbnb's 8-K exhibit shows customer support cost per booking fell about 16% year over year, and the AI assistant now resolves nearly 45% of issues without a human agent.

Chesky told analysts on the call, "It's not about how many tokens you use, it's about the throughput of your product and the quality of your product designs and how much you're shipping." That framing matters because inference costs are small relative to conversion gains at Airbnb's scale.
